evidence.description: The instance retains the timer task.
The weak reference is promoted to a strong self reference before the repeating loop, retaining the instance across suspension points.
Task cancellation is performed only in deinit.

candidates.explanation: Although the task captures self weakly, the guard creates a strong reference that remains alive throughout the repeating loop. Once the guard succeeds, the instance retains the task and the task retains the instance. The deinitializer therefore cannot run to perform the cancellation intended to terminate the task.
candidates.title: Timer task retains its owner indefinitely

evidence.description: The task awaits timePerTree and assigns it to initialInterval, which is never referenced.
The sleep uses a separately fetched interval instead.

candidates.explanation: The initialInterval binding is unused. Its initialization adds an asynchronous read and potential suspension before the first publication without contributing to any calculation or scheduling decision.
candidates.title: Unused initial interval fetch

evidence.description: The interval is multiplied and converted directly to UInt64 without checking its sign, finiteness, or representable range.
The elapsed-time calculation divides by timePerTree and converts the result directly to Int without validation.

candidates.explanation: These floating-point-to-integer conversions can trap for non-finite or out-of-range results; the unsigned conversion also rejects negative values. A zero timePerTree can produce a non-finite tree calculation, and treesAt accepts an unrestricted Date that also affects the result's range. No checks establishing valid conversion inputs are visible. The try? around Task.sleep does not catch numeric conversion traps.
candidates.title: Unchecked numeric conversions can trap
